source: Round 5 states5a: state electrical, plumbing and HVAC/mechanical licensing and statewide code adoption (NEC, plumbing, mechanical/fuel gas editions) for AL-MT jurisdictions, from official state sources

facts.source: Ala. Admin. Code r. 303-X-3-.02 and 303-X-3-.03 (Alabama Electrical Contractors Board, eff. Feb. 14, 2026) - https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/303-X-3
facts.fact: Under Alabama Electrical Contractors Board rules effective February 14, 2026, both electrical contractor and journeyman electrician applicants must document at least 8,000 hours of electrical experience. Each year of an approved apprenticeship or qualifying education can count as 1,000 hours, but no more than 2,000 of the 8,000 hours.
facts.note: Read in the Alabama Administrative Code chapter 303-X-3 (new rules published Dec. 31, 2025, effective Feb. 14, 2026).

facts.source: Alabama Division of Construction Management, State Building Code page - https://dcm.alabama.gov/bldg_code.aspx
facts.fact: Alabama has no statewide electrical code for all buildings. The State Building Code run by the Division of Construction Management (DCM) adopts the 2020 NEC (NFPA 70), effective July 1, 2022, but it covers only state-owned or state-funded projects, public and private K-12 schools, public colleges, hotels/motels and movie theaters. Other homes and commercial buildings follow whatever code the city or county has adopted.
facts.note: DCM page states it has no jurisdiction over residential or commercial property except hotels/motels and movie theaters.

facts.source: Alabama Division of Construction Management, State Building Code page - https://dcm.alabama.gov/bldg_code.aspx
facts.fact: The Alabama State Building Code (Division of Construction Management) adopts the 2021 International Plumbing Code and the 2021 International Fuel Gas Code, effective July 1, 2022. Like the rest of the State Building Code, it applies to state-funded projects, schools, hotels/motels and movie theaters; other buildings use locally adopted codes.

facts.source: Ala. Admin. Code r. 720-X-7-.01(1)(a) (Plumbers and Gas Fitters Examining Board) - https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/720-X-7
facts.fact: Alabama Plumbers and Gas Fitters Examining Board exams are based on the 2021 International Plumbing Code and the 2021 International Fuel Gas Code (rule 720-X-7-.01, last amended effective October 15, 2022).

facts.source: Alabama Division of Construction Management, State Building Code page - https://dcm.alabama.gov/bldg_code.aspx
facts.fact: The Alabama State Building Code uses the 2021 International Mechanical Code, amended March 17, 2025 with portions of the 2024 IMC, and the 2021 International Fuel Gas Code (effective July 1, 2022). It applies only to state-funded projects, schools, hotels/motels and movie theaters; there is no statewide mechanical code for other private buildings.

facts.source: Alabama Board of Heating, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractors, Exam Application EA-1 (2025), quoting Ala. Code 34-31-28 - https://hacr.alabama.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/EA-1-thru-EA-7-Exam-Application-with-Prep-Courses-2025.pdf
facts.fact: Alabama's HVACR board gives two contractor certification exams: HVAC and Refrigeration. To qualify (Ala. Code 34-31-28), an applicant needs 2 or more years as a board-registered apprentice, 3,000 hours of board-approved coursework or experience, or graduation from an approved HVACR program; employer affidavits showing at least 2 years of industry work in the past 5 years are also accepted.

facts.source: Alabama Board of Heating, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractors, Exam Application EA-1 reference lists (2025) - https://hacr.alabama.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/EA-1-thru-EA-7-Exam-Application-with-Prep-Courses-2025.pdf
facts.fact: Alabama's HVAC exam references include the 2021 International Residential Code, ACCA Manual J (8th ed.) and Manual D, and the 2020 NEC. The Refrigeration exam uses the 2021 International Mechanical Code, 29 CFR 1926 and the 2020 NEC. Both also use the NASCLA business and law guide and the Alabama HACR laws and rules.
facts.note: Reference list from the board's 2025 exam application; check for a newer list before testing.

facts.source: 8 AAC 70.025 Minimum electrical standards - https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/alaska/8-AAC-70.025; Alaska DOLWD Mechanical Inspection - https://labor.alaska.gov/lss/mihome.htm
facts.fact: Alaska adopts the 2020 NEC (NFPA 70) as the minimum electrical code for the whole state under 8 AAC 70.025 (last amended effective April 16, 2022), along with the 2017 National Electrical Safety Code (ANSI C2).
facts.note: Both the regulation text and the Department of Labor Mechanical Inspection page list the 2020 NEC.

facts.source: Alaska DOLWD Mechanical Inspection, adopted codes list (8 AAC 63.101) - https://labor.alaska.gov/lss/mihome.htm
facts.fact: Alaska's Department of Labor (Mechanical Inspection Section) adopts the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC) under 8 AAC 63.101, along with the 2018 Uniform Swimming Pool, Spa and Hot Tub Code and the 2018 Uniform Solar Energy, Hydronics and Geothermal Code.
facts.note: The page lists the editions but no effective dates.

facts.source: Alaska Department of Public Safety, Division of Fire and Life Safety, Regulations - https://dps.alaska.gov/Fire/Regulations
facts.fact: The Alaska State Fire Marshal adopted the 2021 International Mechanical Code and 2021 International Fuel Gas Code (together with the 2021 IBC, IEBC and IFC) in 13 AAC 50 through 55, effective October 28, 2022.

facts.source: Alaska DOLWD Mechanical Inspection - https://labor.alaska.gov/lss/mihome.htm
facts.fact: A state-issued Certificate of Fitness (COF) is required to do construction work covered by the NEC anywhere in Alaska. Hours only count toward a journeyman COF if the worker holds a state Electrician or Power Lineman Trainee COF, and plumbers likewise need a Plumber Trainee COF to earn hours toward journeyman.

facts.source: 12 AAC 39 Article 2 (Mechanical Administrator license categories) - https://law.cornell.edu/regulations/alaska/title-12/part-1/chapter-39/article-2; 12 AAC 39.322
facts.fact: Alaska mechanical contractors need a licensed Mechanical Administrator. Current categories are unlimited commercial and industrial plumbing; heating, cooling and process piping; unlimited HVAC/sheet metal; unlimited refrigeration; mechanical systems temperature control; residential plumbing and hydronic heating; and residential HVAC. The residential HVAC category requires journeyman-level residential HVAC experience in at least 2 of the 4 years before applying.

facts.source: Arizona Registrar of Contractors, License Classification Requirements - https://www.azroc.gov/sites/default/files/2023-11/License%20Classification%20Requirements_6.8.20_0.pdf
facts.fact: Arizona ROC electrical licenses R-11 (residential), C-11 (commercial) and CR-11 (dual) each require a qualifying party with 4 years of hands-on and/or managerial experience who passes the Statutes and Rules Exam (SRE) and the trade exam.
facts.note: Experience and exams read on the ROC classification table. Existing KB fact STAT-022 (unverified) covers the lack of a statewide journeyman card.

facts.source: Arizona Registrar of Contractors, License Classification Requirements - https://www.azroc.gov/sites/default/files/2023-11/License%20Classification%20Requirements_6.8.20_0.pdf
facts.fact: Arizona ROC plumbing licenses R-37 (residential, including solar), C-37 (commercial) and CR-37 (dual) each require 4 years of hands-on and/or managerial experience plus the Statutes and Rules Exam and the trade exam. Because R-37 includes solar work, it also requires the Solar exam.

facts.source: Arizona Registrar of Contractors, License Classification Requirements - https://www.azroc.gov/sites/default/files/2023-11/License%20Classification%20Requirements_6.8.20_0.pdf
facts.fact: Arizona ROC air conditioning and refrigeration licenses are R-39 (residential, including solar), C-39 (commercial) and CR-39 (dual). Each requires 4 years of hands-on and/or managerial experience plus the Statutes and Rules Exam and the trade exam, and R-39 also requires the Solar exam.

facts.source: Mike Holt NEC Adoption List - https://www.mikeholt.com/necadoptionlist.php; IAEI Code Adoption by State - https://www.iaei.org/page/nec-code-adoption
facts.fact: Arizona does not adopt the NEC at the state level. Each city or county adopts its own electrical code edition, so the NEC edition an Arizona electrician works under depends on the local jurisdiction.
facts.note: Two respected trade references (Mike Holt and IAEI) agree; no state agency adopts the NEC for private work.

facts.source: ICC Code Adoptions Map, Arizona - https://www.iccsafe.org/advocacy/adoptions-map/arizona/
facts.fact: Arizona has no statewide plumbing or mechanical code for private construction. Codes are adopted locally, mostly the I-codes (such as the IPC, IMC and IFGC), so the edition depends on the city or county. The only statewide code ICC notes is the State Fire Code (2018 IFC).
facts.note: ICC adoption page: 'Codes are adopted locally in Arizona and are predominantly the I-codes.'

facts.source: Arkansas DOLL, 2023 NEC Rule Summary and Public Notice (July 2024) - https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023-NEC-Rule-Summary.pdf; Arkansas Building Authority Current Codes (rev. Jan. 2023) - https://sas.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/CurrentCodes072023.pdf
facts.fact: Arkansas adopts the NEC statewide through the Board of Electrical Examiners (Rule 010.13-008). The state listed the 2020 Arkansas NEC as current in 2023, and in 2024 the board proposed moving to the 2023 NEC while keeping Article 210 at the 2020 standard. Confirm the edition now in force with the Department of Labor and Licensing.
facts.note: No official page read confirms which edition is in force today. IAEI lists 2020 NEC effective 8/1/2022; Mike Holt's list shows the 2026 NEC effective 9/3/2026.

facts.source: Arkansas Building Authority, Current Codes (rev. Jan. 2023) - https://sas.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/CurrentCodes072023.pdf; Arkansas Dept. of Health, Plumbing and Natural Gas - https://healthy.arkansas.gov/programs-services/licensing-military-member-licensure-permits-plan-reviews/plumbing-natural-gas-health-code/
facts.fact: Arkansas plumbing and gas work follows state codes administered by the Arkansas Department of Health: the 2018 Arkansas Plumbing Code (a state code published by ICC) and the 2018 Arkansas Fuel Gas Code. Plumbers are licensed by the Health Department's State Committee of Plumbing Examiners.
facts.note: Editions from the state's 2023 current-codes list; ADH page confirms the codes are ICC-published but gives no edition, so check for a newer adoption.

facts.source: Arkansas Dept. of Health, Plumbing Licensing Rules (eff. Sept. 5, 2024), Section II - https://healthy.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/Plumbing-Licensing-Rules.pdf
facts.fact: In Arkansas, a journeyman plumber applicant needs at least 4 years of experience (or its equivalent) and a master plumber applicant needs at least 5 years. A journeyman must hold that license for one full year before becoming eligible for the master exam (the committee may waive this for extreme hardship).

facts.source: 17 CAR Part 261 (HVACR Licensing Board rules), sec. 261-103 and 261-104, as posted by Arkansas DOLL - https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/17CARpt.261-Clean.pdf
facts.fact: Arkansas HVACR licenses: Class A has no capacity limit; Class B is limited to air conditioning of 25 tons or less and heating of 1,000,000 BTUH input or less per unit, and refrigeration of 15 hp or less per unit; Class D covers sheet metal ductwork only; Class E covers refrigeration only. Exam applicants need at least 2 years of experience as or for an HVACR contractor, and employees who do HVACR work must hold a registration.
facts.note: Class definitions read in the DOLL-posted 17 CAR Part 261 rule text (clean copy); confirm this is the final adopted version.

facts.source: 17 CAR 261-121(a) - https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/17CARpt.261-Clean.pdf; Arkansas Building Authority Current Codes - https://sas.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/CurrentCodes072023.pdf
facts.fact: The Arkansas HVACR Licensing Board adopts the 2021 International Mechanical Code as the state mechanical code, administered by the Department of Labor and Licensing.
facts.note: Both the board rule text and the state's current-codes list name the 2021 IMC.

facts.source: California Building Standards Commission, Codes page - https://www.dgs.ca.gov/bsc/codes; HCD 01/23 Initial Statement of Reasons, Part 3 - https://www.dgs.ca.gov/-/media/Divisions/BSC/03-Rulemaking/2024-Triennial-Cycle/CAC/2024-03-25-PEME/HCD-01-23-ISOR-PT3.pdf
facts.fact: California's electrical code is the California Electrical Code (Title 24, Part 3). The current 2025 California Electrical Code, effective January 1, 2026, is based on the 2023 NEC with California amendments.
facts.note: BSC page gives the 2025 Title 24 effective date of Jan. 1, 2026; the state rulemaking document says the 2025 CEC is based on the 2023 NEC.

facts.source: California Building Standards Commission, Codes page - https://www.dgs.ca.gov/bsc/codes; BSC 02/24 Initial Statement of Reasons, Part 5 - https://www.dgs.ca.gov/-/media/Divisions/BSC/03-Rulemaking/2024-Triennial-Cycle/CAC/2024-03-25-PEME/BSC-02-24-ISOR-PT5.pdf
facts.fact: The 2025 California Plumbing Code (Title 24, Part 5), effective January 1, 2026, is based on the 2024 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC) published by IAPMO, not the IPC.

facts.source: California Building Standards Commission, Codes page - https://www.dgs.ca.gov/bsc/codes; BSC 01/24 Initial Statement of Reasons, Part 4 - https://www.dgs.ca.gov/-/media/Divisions/BSC/03-Rulemaking/2024-Triennial-Cycle/CAC/2024-03-25-PEME/BSC-01-24-ISOR-PT4.pdf
facts.fact: The 2025 California Mechanical Code (Title 24, Part 4), effective January 1, 2026, is based on the 2024 Uniform Mechanical Code (UMC) published by IAPMO, not the IMC.

facts.source: California DIR, Electrician Certification application form - https://www.dir.ca.gov/das/ElectricalCertificationForm.pdf
facts.fact: California's Department of Industrial Relations certifies electricians by category with minimum experience hours: General Electrician 8,000 hours, Residential Electrician 4,800, Fire/Life Safety Technician 4,000, Voice Data Video Technician 4,000, and Nonresidential Lighting Technician 2,000. An approved applicant must take the exam within 1 year of being notified of eligibility.

facts.source: CSLB, Acceptable documentation of journey-level experience - https://www.cslb.ca.gov/Resources/Contractors/Journeymen/AcceptableDocs.pdf
facts.fact: California licenses plumbing businesses as CSLB C-36 Plumbing contractors. The qualifying individual must show at least 4 years of journey-level experience in that classification within the last 10 years and pass the exams.
facts.note: Experience rule read on the CSLB document.

facts.source: CSLB, Acceptable documentation of journey-level experience - https://www.cslb.ca.gov/Resources/Contractors/Journeymen/AcceptableDocs.pdf
facts.fact: California HVAC businesses are licensed by CSLB as C-20 Warm-Air Heating, Ventilating and Air-Conditioning contractors. As with every CSLB classification, the qualifier needs at least 4 years of journey-level experience in the trade within the last 10 years and must pass the exams.

facts.source: Colorado State Electrical Board (DORA) homepage - https://dpo.colorado.gov/Electrical; IAEI Colorado NEC adoption - https://www.iaei.org/page/colorado-electrical-ceus
facts.fact: The Colorado State Electrical Board adopts the NEC statewide by rule (Rule 1.5, incorporation by reference), and the state runs electrical inspections where there is no local enforcement. The board adopted the 2023 NEC effective August 1, 2023, and held a May 27, 2026 rulemaking hearing to adopt the 2026 NEC. Check the board for the 2026 effective date.
facts.note: DORA page confirms the May 27, 2026 hearing to adopt the 2026 NEC but gives no effective date; Mike Holt's list shows Aug. 1, 2026. The 2023 date comes from IAEI.

facts.source: 3 CCR 720-1, Rule 2 (Colorado Plumbing Board) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/colorado/700/720/rule-3-ccr-720-1/section-3-ccr-720-1-2; ICC press release July 19, 2023
facts.fact: Colorado has a statewide plumbing code adopted by the State Plumbing Board: the 2021 International Plumbing Code and the 2021 International Fuel Gas Code with Colorado amendments (published as the 2021 Colorado Plumbing and Fuel Gas Codes).
facts.note: Regulation text (current through June 2025) incorporates the 2021 IPC and 2021 IFGC; ICC's July 2023 release confirms the board's adoption. Check for a later 2024 update.

facts.source: ICC Code Adoptions Map, Colorado - https://www.iccsafe.org/advocacy/adoptions-map/colorado/
facts.fact: Colorado has no statewide building or mechanical code; mechanical codes such as the IMC are adopted and enforced by local governments. State-level exceptions are state-owned buildings, public K-12 schools and health facilities, factory-built homes, and hotels, motels and multifamily buildings in areas with no local code.
facts.note: ICC adoption page: 'Colorado has no statewide building code.' Plumbing and electrical are the exceptions, with statewide codes set by their boards.

facts.source: CT DAS Office of State Building Inspector, Connecticut State Building Code - https://portal.ct.gov/en/DAS/Office-of-State-Building-Inspector/Connecticut-State-Building-Code/Regulations
facts.fact: Connecticut's statewide building code is the 2022 Connecticut State Building Code, which applies to permit applications filed on or after October 1, 2022. It adopts the 2020 NEC (NFPA 70) for electrical work.
facts.note: The DAS page lists no newer code; Mike Holt notes a 2023 NEC update process underway with no effective date set.

facts.source: CT DAS Office of State Building Inspector, Connecticut State Building Code - https://portal.ct.gov/en/DAS/Office-of-State-Building-Inspector/Connecticut-State-Building-Code/Regulations
facts.fact: The 2022 Connecticut State Building Code (permit applications filed from October 1, 2022) adopts the 2021 International Plumbing Code as Connecticut's statewide plumbing code.

facts.source: CT DAS Office of State Building Inspector, Connecticut State Building Code - https://portal.ct.gov/en/DAS/Office-of-State-Building-Inspector/Connecticut-State-Building-Code/Regulations
facts.fact: The 2022 Connecticut State Building Code (permit applications filed from October 1, 2022) adopts the 2021 International Mechanical Code, along with the 2021 IBC, IRC, IEBC and IECC.

facts.source: CT DCP, Electrical License Types and Scope of Work - https://portal.ct.gov/DCP/Occupational-and-Professional-Division/Occupational--Profess/Electrical-License-Types-and-Scope-of-Work
facts.fact: In Connecticut, an E-2 Unlimited Electrical Journeyperson needs a completed registered apprenticeship (or at least 4 years of equivalent experience and training) and may work only while employed by a licensed contractor. An E-1 Unlimited Electrical Contractor needs 2 years as a licensed unlimited journeyperson (or 6 years of equivalent experience and training). Limited licenses include C-5 (up to 48 volts or 8 amps), L-5 (up to 25 volts or 5 amps) and PV-1 solar.

facts.source: CT DCP, Plumbing Licenses and Scope of Work - https://portal.ct.gov/DCP/Occupational-and-Professional-Division/Occupational--Profess/Plumbing-Licenses-and-Scope-of-Work
facts.fact: Connecticut's P-2 Unlimited Journeyperson Plumber needs a completed registered apprenticeship (or equivalent experience and training) and works only for a licensed contractor; the P-1 Unlimited Plumbing Contractor needs 2 years as an unlimited licensed journeyperson. Limited categories include J-1/J-2 well pumps and water conditioning and P-6/P-7 sewer, storm and water piping.

facts.source: CT DCP, Heating, Piping and Cooling License Types and Scope of Work - https://portal.ct.gov/DCP/Occupational-and-Professional-Division/Occupational--Profess/Heating-Piping-and-Cooling-License-Types-and-Scope-of-Work
facts.fact: Connecticut heating and cooling contractor licenses (S-1 unlimited, D-1 warm air/AC/refrigeration, B-1 gas and oil burner, G-1 gas piping) each require 2 years as a properly licensed journeyperson or equivalent experience; the matching journeyperson licenses (S-2, D-2, B-2, G-2) require a registered apprenticeship or equivalent. D-1 work excludes oil burners, and B-1 'light commercial' means burners of 5 gallons per hour or less or a total heating load up to 500,000 BTU.

facts.source: Delaware State Fire Marshal, 2026 DSFPR update (Regulation 701) - https://statefiremarshal.delaware.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/110/2025/12/2026-DSFPR-update.pdf; IAEI Delaware page
facts.fact: Delaware's 2026 State Fire Prevention Regulations (Regulation 701), effective January 1, 2026, list NFPA 70, the 2023 NEC, as the electrical code.
facts.note: Effective date and edition read on the State Fire Marshal's 2026 DSFPR update. IAEI adds that local jurisdictions must adopt the NEC enacted by the Fire Prevention Commission.

facts.source: 16 Del. Admin. Code 4455-1.0 and 2.0 (State of Delaware Plumbing Code) - https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/delaware/16-Del-Admin-Code-SS-4455-2.0; 26 DE Reg. 110 (Aug. 1, 2022)
facts.fact: The State of Delaware Plumbing Code, issued by the Division of Public Health (16 Del. Admin. Code 4455), adopts the 2021 International Plumbing Code with Delaware amendments, effective August 11, 2022.
facts.note: Final order in 26 DE Reg. 110 sets the Aug. 11, 2022 effective date; codified text names the 2021 IPC.

facts.source: Delaware State Fire Marshal, 2026 DSFPR update (Regulation 701) - https://statefiremarshal.delaware.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/110/2025/12/2026-DSFPR-update.pdf
facts.fact: Delaware's 2026 State Fire Prevention Regulations (effective January 1, 2026) list NFPA 54 National Fuel Gas Code (2024 edition), NFPA 58 LP-Gas Code (2024 edition) and NFPA 96 commercial cooking ventilation (2024 edition) among the adopted codes.

facts.source: 24 Del. C. 1802(11)-(12) - https://delcode.delaware.gov/title24/c018/sc01/index.html
facts.fact: Delaware licenses Master HVACR licensees for heating, ventilation, air conditioning, refrigeration, hydronics, commercial hoods and gas piping. A Master HVACR Restricted license covers only one area: forced-air heating and gas piping, hydronic heating and gas piping, commercial hood systems, refrigeration, air conditioning, or gas piping.

facts.source: DC Department of Buildings, 2017 DC Construction Codes - https://dob.dc.gov/node/1615636
facts.fact: The District of Columbia's current construction codes are the 2017 DC Construction Codes, effective May 29, 2020. The DC Electrical Code (12C DCMR) is based on the 2014 NEC. DOB began work in 2026 on new codes based on the 2024 model codes, with final rules expected in late 2027.
facts.note: Current codes read on DOB page; the 2024-code update timeline is from a June 25, 2026 news report on DOB's listening sessions.

facts.source: DC Department of Buildings, 2017 DC Construction Codes - https://dob.dc.gov/node/1615636
facts.fact: Under the 2017 DC Construction Codes (effective May 29, 2020), the DC Plumbing Code (12F DCMR) is based on the 2015 International Plumbing Code.

facts.source: DC Department of Buildings, 2017 DC Construction Codes - https://dob.dc.gov/node/1615636
facts.fact: Under the 2017 DC Construction Codes (effective May 29, 2020), the DC Mechanical Code (12E DCMR) is based on the 2015 International Mechanical Code and the DC Fuel Gas Code (12D DCMR) on the 2015 International Fuel Gas Code.

facts.source: DC DLCP Electrician license guide - https://dlcp.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/DLCP/publication/attachments/Electrician.pdf
facts.fact: DC electricians are licensed as apprentice, journeyman and master. A journeyman by exam needs 4 years (8,000 work hours) and a master needs 8 years (16,000 hours). Proof of completing a nationally certified apprenticeship can waive the journeyman exam, and the exams are open book.
facts.note: The DLCP guide lists the 2011 NEC as the study reference, which may be out of date; confirm the current exam code edition.

facts.source: DC DLCP Plumbing and Gasfitting license guide - https://dlcp.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/DLCP/publication/attachments/PlumbingGasfitting.pdf
facts.fact: DC plumbers and gasfitters are licensed as apprentice, journeyman and master. A journeyman needs 4 years (8,000 work hours) and a master needs 8 years (16,000 hours), verified by tax records and employer letters signed off by a master. Completing a nationally certified apprenticeship can waive the journeyman exam, and the exams are open book on the IPC and IFGC.
facts.note: The DLCP guide lists the 2012 IPC and IFGC as exam references, which may be out of date.

facts.source: Florida Building Commission, 2026 FBC Workplan (Aug. 2026) - https://www.floridabuilding.org/fbc/commission/FBC_0726/Commission/2026_FBC_Workplan_August_2026.pdf; IAEI and Mike Holt NEC adoption lists
facts.fact: Florida's electrical code is set in the statewide Florida Building Code. The 8th Edition (2023) FBC, effective December 31, 2023, uses the 2020 NEC. The 9th Edition (2026) FBC, built on the 2024 I-Codes and the 2023 NEC, takes effect December 31, 2026.
facts.note: 9th Edition date and model codes read on the Commission's workplan; the 8th Edition's 2020 NEC comes from IAEI and Mike Holt, which agree.

facts.source: Florida Building Commission, 2026 FBC Workplan (Aug. 2026) - https://www.floridabuilding.org/fbc/commission/FBC_0726/Commission/2026_FBC_Workplan_August_2026.pdf; Alachua County Codes page
facts.fact: Florida enforces a statewide Florida Building Code - Plumbing. The 8th Edition (2023) has been in effect since December 31, 2023, and the 9th Edition (2026), based on the 2024 International Plumbing Code with Florida changes, takes effect December 31, 2026.

facts.source: Florida Building Commission, 2026 FBC Workplan (Aug. 2026) - https://www.floridabuilding.org/fbc/commission/FBC_0726/Commission/2026_FBC_Workplan_August_2026.pdf
facts.fact: The Florida Building Code - Mechanical and - Fuel Gas apply statewide. For the 9th Edition (2026) FBC, effective December 31, 2026, the Florida Building Commission based them on the 2024 International Mechanical Code and 2024 International Fuel Gas Code.

facts.source: Fla. Stat. 489.105(3)(f)-(g), as amended by Laws of Fla. ch. 2024-206 - https://laws.flrules.org/2024/206
facts.fact: Florida licenses air-conditioning contractors in classes. A Class A air-conditioning contractor is unlimited, while a Class B contractor is limited to 25 tons of cooling and 500,000 Btu of heating in any one system.

facts.source: Fla. Stat. 489.111(2)(c) - https://m.flsenate.gov/Statutes/489.111
facts.fact: To sit for a Florida Construction Industry Licensing Board exam (including plumbing, mechanical and air-conditioning contractor), an applicant generally needs 4 years of experience as a skilled worker or foreman with at least 1 year as a foreman, or a 4-year engineering, architecture or building construction degree plus 1 year of experience, or college credit combined with foreman experience. Full-time years are counted at 2,000 person-hours.

facts.source: Georgia DCA, Current Codes 'green sheet' (Jan. 1, 2026) - https://dca.georgia.gov/document/document/green-sheet-current-codes-greenpdf/download; DCA memo Dec. 1, 2025
facts.fact: Georgia's State Minimum Standard Electrical Code is the 2023 NEC with Georgia amendments (in effect since January 1, 2025; 2026 Georgia amendments took effect January 1, 2026). Because Georgia omits the IRC's electrical chapters, the NEC also applies to one- and two-family dwellings.

facts.source: Georgia DCA memo, New Codes and Amendments Effective January 1, 2026 - https://dca.georgia.gov/document/document/new-codes-and-amendments-effective-january-1-2026-memo/download
facts.fact: Since January 1, 2026, Georgia's State Minimum Standard Plumbing Code is the 2024 International Plumbing Code with Georgia amendments. The IRC's plumbing provisions are omitted in Georgia, so the IPC also governs one- and two-family dwellings.

facts.source: Georgia DCA memo, New Codes and Amendments Effective January 1, 2026 - https://dca.georgia.gov/document/document/new-codes-and-amendments-effective-january-1-2026-memo/download
facts.fact: Since January 1, 2026, Georgia's State Minimum Standard Mechanical and Gas Codes are the 2024 International Mechanical Code and 2024 International Fuel Gas Code, each with Georgia amendments.

facts.source: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 121-3-.01 (Statewide Electrical Contractor License) - https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/georgia/Ga-Comp-R-Regs-R-121-3-.01
facts.fact: Georgia issues statewide electrical contractor licenses in two classes: Class I (restricted) covers single-phase installations not over 200 amperes at the service drop or lateral, and Class II is unrestricted. Applicants must be at least 21, document at least 4 years of primary electrical experience (Class II must include work above single-phase 200-amp systems) and score at least 70 on the exam.

facts.source: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 121-3-.02(4)-(5) - https://rules.sos.ga.gov/GAC/121-3; Georgia SOS Master and Journeyman Plumbers FAQ - https://sos.ga.gov/page/division-master-and-journeyman-plumbers-faq
facts.fact: Georgia's journeyman plumber license requires at least 1 year of plumbing experience. Master plumbers (Class I and Class II) need at least 5 years of plumbing experience, 2 of them as a licensed journeyman, and Class II also requires commercial or industrial experience. Class I is limited to single-family and one-level two-family dwellings and commercial buildings up to 10,000 square feet. Exams are given by PSI.

facts.source: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 121-3-.04 - https://rules.sos.ga.gov/GAC/121-3
facts.fact: Georgia Conditioned Air Contractor Class I (restricted) licenses cover systems of no more than 175,000 BTU of heating and 60,000 BTU (5 tons) of cooling and require 4 years of experience. Class II (unrestricted) requires 5 years of experience, including systems above those limits.

facts.source: Hawaii State Building Code Council, State Electrical Code (proposed rule text) - https://ags.hawaii.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/StateElectricalCode_PROPOSED.pdf; IAEI and Mike Holt NEC adoption lists
facts.fact: Hawaii's State Building Code Council adopts a State Electrical Code based on the 2020 NEC (listed as effective March 14, 2023). Permits and enforcement are handled by the counties, which adopt the state codes by ordinance.
facts.note: Council rule text names the 2020 NEC; IAEI and Mike Holt both list 2020 NEC effective 3/14/2023. County adoption dates vary.

facts.source: Hawaii Administrative Rules, State Plumbing Code, Adoption of the Uniform Plumbing Code - https://regulations.justia.com/states/hawaii/title-3/building-code-council/state-plumbing-code/adoption-of-the-uniform-plumbing-code
facts.fact: Hawaii's State Plumbing Code, adopted by the State Building Code Council, is based on the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC) with appendices. As with other state codes, the counties adopt and enforce it locally.
facts.note: Rule text current through April 2025; check for a newer UPC adoption.

facts.source: HRS 448E-5(b) - https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol10_Ch0436-0474/HRS0448E/HRS_0448E-0005.htm
facts.fact: Under HRS 448E-5, a Hawaii journey worker electrician needs 5 years (at least 10,000 hours) of supervised wiring experience plus 240 hours of electrical coursework accepted by a University of Hawaii community college. A supervising electrician must have been a journey worker electrician for 4 years. Specialty (3 years/6,000 hours), industrial (4 years/8,000 hours) and maintenance electrician licenses also exist.
facts.note: Requirements in subsection (b), effective July 1, 2013.

facts.source: HRS 448E-5(b) - https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol10_Ch0436-0474/HRS0448E/HRS_0448E-0005.htm
facts.fact: In Hawaii, a journey worker plumber needs 5 years (at least 10,000 hours) of experience as a helper to a journey worker or master plumber. A master plumber must have been registered as a journey worker plumber for 2 years (or have equivalent experience).

facts.source: Haw. Code R. tit. 16, ch. 77, subch. 19, exh. A (Specialty Contractor Classifications) - https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/hawaii/Haw-Code-R-tit-16-ch-77-subch-19-exh-A
facts.fact: Hawaii licenses HVAC businesses through the Contractors License Board as C-52 Ventilating and Air Conditioning contractors (warm-air heating, air cooling and complete ventilating and AC systems). Refrigeration work is the separate C-40 Refrigeration classification, while electrical and plumbing contractors are C-13 and C-37.

facts.source: Idaho DOPL communication, 2023 Code Enforcement Implementation (June 2024) - https://admws.idaho.gov/pipermail/dopl-communication/2024-June/000027.html
facts.fact: Idaho's Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses moved to the 2023 NEC effective April 19, 2024 (with exceptions set by rule), with full enforcement no later than January 1, 2025. Permits issued before April 19, 2024 are inspected under the 2017 NEC.
facts.note: IAEI and Mike Holt list different dates (7/1/2023 and 7/1/2024); the DOPL notice is the official source.

facts.source: Idaho Code 54-2601 - https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title54/T54CH26/SECT54-2601; IDAPA 24.39.20.600
facts.fact: Idaho law requires plumbing to follow the Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC) published by IAPMO, adopted with amendments by the Idaho Plumbing Board as the Idaho State Plumbing Code. A newly adopted edition takes effect January 1 of the year after the board adopts it.
facts.note: Edition caveat: IDAPA 24.39.20.600 (eff. 3/28/2023) adopted the 2015 UPC, and board minutes from Oct. 2023 show it discussing a 2024 UPC-based code. Confirm the edition in force.

facts.source: IDAPA 24.39.70.600 (Idaho HVAC Board, adopted codes) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/idaho/24/24-39-70/section-24-39-70-600
facts.fact: The Idaho HVAC Board adopts the 2018 International Mechanical Code and 2018 International Fuel Gas Code with Idaho amendments, plus Parts V (Mechanical) and VI (Fuel Gas) of the 2018 IRC for one- and two-family dwellings (rule effective March 28, 2023).
facts.note: Rule text current through June 2025; check for a newer adoption.

facts.source: Mike Holt NEC Adoption List - https://www.mikeholt.com/necadoptionlist.php; IAEI Code Adoption by State - https://www.iaei.org/page/nec-code-adoption; 65 ILCS 5/11-33-1
facts.fact: Illinois has no statewide electrician license and no statewide NEC adoption. Electrical contractor registration or licensing and the NEC edition in use are set by each municipality or county.
facts.note: Mike Holt and IAEI agree there is no statewide adoption; both mention a 2008 NEC rule for commercial buildings outside local code areas, which was not confirmed on a state page.

facts.source: 77 Ill. Adm. Code 890 (Illinois Plumbing Code) - https://ilga.gov/ftp/JCAR/AdminCode/077/077008900A01300R.html; IDPH local ordinance review letter quoting Illinois Plumbing License Law Sec. 42
facts.fact: Illinois has a statewide minimum plumbing code written by the Illinois Department of Public Health: the Illinois Plumbing Code (77 Ill. Adm. Code 890), last broadly amended in 2014. It is a state-written code, not the IPC or UPC. The power to set the minimum plumbing code belongs to IDPH and cannot be taken over by local governments, including home-rule units.

facts.source: No state HVAC licensing agency identified; local building departments
facts.fact: Illinois does not issue a statewide HVAC or mechanical contractor license, and there is no statewide mechanical code for private buildings. HVAC licensing and mechanical code adoption are handled by cities and counties.
facts.note: Not confirmed on an official state page; based on the absence of a state HVAC board. EPA 608 certification still applies to refrigerant work.

facts.source: IAEI Indiana page - https://www.iaei.org/page/indiana-electrical-ceus; Mike Holt state license page (IN) - https://www.mikeholt.com/statelicense.php?id=IN
facts.fact: Indiana does not license electricians at the state level; electrical licensing is handled by cities and counties (for example, Indianapolis). However, local jurisdictions may not adopt or enforce their own electrical code unless the state Fire Prevention and Building Safety Commission approves it.
facts.note: Two trade references (IAEI and Mike Holt) agree.
keywords: fire prevention and building safety commission

facts.source: Indiana DHS, Electrical Code Regulatory Analysis (draft) - https://www.in.gov/dhs/files/Electrical-Code-Regulatory-Analysis-DRAFT.pdf; IAEI Indiana page
facts.fact: Indiana's statewide Indiana Electrical Code (675 IAC 17-1.8) is the 2009 edition, based on the 2008 NEC and effective August 26, 2009, for commercial buildings; homes built under the Indiana Residential Code use 2017 NEC-based rules (effective December 26, 2019). A 2026 Indiana Electrical Code based on the 2023 NEC was in rulemaking in 2026.
facts.note: DHS analysis confirms the 2009 code is current and proposes a 2026 code (proposed effective Jan. 1, 2026), but no page read confirms whether the new code has taken effect. Mike Holt lists it as underway.

facts.fact: Indiana's statewide plumbing code is the 2012 Indiana Plumbing Code (675 IAC 16), based on the 2006 International Plumbing Code and effective December 24, 2012. In 2026 the state proposed amendments to it (public hearing June 25, 2026); adoption and effective date were still pending in August 2026.
facts.note: Model-code basis and effective date from the IDHS code list (city copy); DHS docket confirms the 2012 code is the existing code.

facts.source: IDHS code list as published by City of Decatur - https://www.cityofdecatur.in.gov/Documents/Building Codes per IDHS (002).pdf
facts.fact: Indiana's statewide mechanical and fuel gas codes are the 2014 Indiana Mechanical Code (675 IAC 18, based on the 2012 IMC) and the 2014 Indiana Fuel Gas Code (675 IAC 25, based on the 2012 IFGC), effective December 1, 2014. Indiana has no state HVAC license; HVAC contractors are licensed locally.
facts.note: Single undated local copy of the IDHS list; the state DHS code page could not be loaded to confirm no newer edition. No-state-license point not confirmed on a state page.

facts.source: Iowa DIAL, Electrical Permits and Inspections (Adoption Notice of the 2023 NEC effective July 1, 2025; HF 2800 notice) - https://dial.iowa.gov/electrical-permits-inspections
facts.fact: Iowa enforces the NEC statewide for all electrical installations. The 2023 NEC took effect July 1, 2025, and House File 2800 (signed and effective June 2, 2026) removed the earlier state amendments in 481 IAC 404.3, so Iowa now uses the 2023 NEC without those amendments (apart from exclusions written into HF 2800) until the 2026 NEC is adopted.
facts.note: Read on the DIAL electrical permits page in October 2026.

facts.source: Iowa Plumbing and Mechanical Systems Board, ARC 8913C (adopted Jan. 29, 2025) - https://rules.iowa.gov/Notice/Details/8913C; 641 IAC 25.2
facts.fact: Iowa's state plumbing code is the 2024 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC) with Iowa amendments, effective March 26, 2025 (replacing the 2021 UPC). The state code applies to plumbing throughout Iowa; local jurisdictions may not adopt a different plumbing code and may add amendments only if they are stricter.
facts.note: Adoption and effective date from ARC 8913C; local-amendment rule from 641 IAC 25.2.

facts.source: Iowa Admin. Code r. 641-61.2 (state mechanical code, eff. 3/26/2025) - https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/iowa/Iowa-Admin-Code-r-641-61.2
facts.fact: Iowa's state mechanical code adopts Sections 101 and 102 and Chapters 2 through 15 of the 2024 International Mechanical Code by reference, effective March 26, 2025.

facts.source: K.S.A. 12-1525 - https://ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch12/012_015_0025.html; K.S.A. 12-1526 - https://codes.findlaw.com/ks/chapter-12-cities-and-municipalities/ks-st-sect-12-1526/
facts.fact: Kansas has no state electrician license; counties and cities that choose to license electricians do so under K.S.A. 12-1525 and 12-1526, using standard exams from ICC, IAPMO or Prometric with a 75% passing score. Journeyman and residential certificates need 2 years of supervised field experience (no more than 1 year from trade school of at least 930 hours), and a master needs a journeyman certificate held at least 2 years. A license is valid in any other Kansas city or county that requires licensure.
facts.note: A 2026 bill for statewide electrician licensing (HB 2588) died in the Legislature.

facts.source: Kansas Statutes Chapter 12, Article 15 (K.S.A. 12-1508 to 12-1511) - https://kslegislature.gov/laws/012_000_0000_chapter/012_015_0000_article/; Kansas AG Opinion 1999-42
facts.fact: Kansas does not license plumbers statewide. Cities and counties that require plumber licensing use the standard competency exams designated by K.S.A. 12-1508, and a Kansas Attorney General opinion (1999-42) says a city may not use home rule to add licensing requirements for plumbers, electricians or mechanical contractors.
facts.note: Based on statute section titles and the AG opinion summary listed with K.S.A. 12-1525; full plumbing section text not read.

facts.source: Kansas Statutes Chapter 12, Article 15 (K.S.A. 12-1540 to 12-1544) - https://kslegislature.gov/laws/012_000_0000_chapter/012_015_0000_article/
facts.fact: Kansas has no state HVAC license. K.S.A. 12-1540 to 12-1544 set the framework for cities and counties that license mechanical (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) contractors, masters and journeymen, including designated standard exams, field experience and reciprocal agreements.
facts.note: Based on statute section titles; full text not read.

facts.source: Mike Holt NEC Adoption List - https://www.mikeholt.com/necadoptionlist.php; IAEI Code Adoption by State - https://www.iaei.org/page/nec-code-adoption
facts.fact: Kansas has no statewide NEC adoption for private buildings; each city or county adopts and enforces its own electrical code edition. The state adopted an NEC edition only for state-owned buildings.
facts.note: Mike Holt and IAEI agree (state-owned building adoption dated 2011, 2008 NEC per Mike Holt).

facts.source: Kentucky Dept. of Housing, Buildings and Construction, 2023 NEC Update Announcement (Oct. 7, 2024) - https://dhbc.ky.gov/Documents/2023 NEC Update Announcement.pdf
facts.fact: Kentucky began mandatory enforcement of the 2023 NEC on January 1, 2025. For one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses, NEC 210.52(C), 230.67 and 314.27(C) were not mandatory until July 15, 2026, and certain GFCI rules in 210.8(A) and 210.8(D)(8)-(11) are on hold until the related UL standards are revised.

facts.source: Kentucky DHBC, Find Currently Enforced Code - https://dhbc.ky.gov/Documents/Find Currently Enforced Code.pdf
facts.fact: Kentucky does not use the IPC or UPC. Its statewide plumbing rules are the Kentucky State Plumbing Law, Regulations and Code in 815 KAR Chapter 20, a state-written code enforced by the Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction.

facts.source: Kentucky DHBC, Find Currently Enforced Code - https://dhbc.ky.gov/Documents/Find Currently Enforced Code.pdf; 815 KAR 7:125
facts.fact: Kentucky's currently enforced codes list the 2015 International Mechanical Code and the 2012 NFPA 54 National Fuel Gas Code, alongside the 2018 Kentucky Building Code and 2018 Kentucky Residential Code (both based on the 2015 I-Codes).
facts.note: From the undated DHBC 'currently enforced code' list; DHBC has a task force working on newer building and residential codes, so check for updates.

facts.source: Louisiana Uniform Construction Code Council, Louisiana Construction Code Information (rev. Aug. 6, 2026) - http://luccc.louisiana.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/LSUCCC_Louisiana-Construction-Code-Information.pdf; LUCCC homepage
facts.fact: Louisiana enforces the 2020 NEC statewide as part of the Louisiana State Uniform Construction Code, effective January 1, 2023. A proposed rule to move to the 2023 NEC and the 2024 I-Codes was published in the August 20, 2026 Louisiana Register.

facts.source: Louisiana Uniform Construction Code Council, Louisiana Construction Code Information (rev. Aug. 6, 2026) - http://luccc.louisiana.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/LSUCCC_Louisiana-Construction-Code-Information.pdf
facts.fact: Louisiana's statewide plumbing code is the International Plumbing Code, which replaced the old Louisiana State Plumbing Code on January 1, 2016. The current Uniform Construction Code uses the 2021 ICC codes with Louisiana amendments, effective January 1, 2023.
facts.note: The LUCCC sheet lists the 2021 IPC under the 2021 ICC codes without a separate date; Jan. 1, 2023 is the date for the 2021 ICC package.

facts.source: Louisiana Uniform Construction Code Council, Louisiana Construction Code Information (rev. Aug. 6, 2026) - http://luccc.louisiana.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/LSUCCC_Louisiana-Construction-Code-Information.pdf
facts.fact: Louisiana's Uniform Construction Code includes the 2021 International Mechanical Code and 2021 International Fuel Gas Code, effective January 1, 2023, with mandatory statewide enforcement.

facts.source: La. R.S. 37:1367 - https://legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=93229
facts.fact: Under La. R.S. 37:1367, a Louisiana journeyman plumber must hold a board license and work for a licensed master plumber, apprentices must work under a licensed journeyman, and a master plumber must hold or have held a journeyman plumber license. Journeymen who worked independently before January 1, 2024 got five years to pass the master exam.
facts.note: Licensing moves to the LSLBC plumbing subcommittee on Jan. 1, 2027 under Act 908 of 2026 (see existing KB fact STAT-159).

facts.source: IAEI Louisiana page - https://www.iaei.org/page/louisiana-electrical-ceus
facts.fact: Louisiana does not license individual electricians statewide; requirements are set locally (for example, New Orleans requires ICC certifications). Electrical contracting businesses are licensed by the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors.
facts.note: Only one trade reference (IAEI) read for the no-state-license point; LSLBC dollar thresholds for electrical work not confirmed.

facts.source: 02-318 CMR ch. 120 (Electricians' Examining Board, Electrical Installation Standards) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/maine/02/318/chapter-120/; IAEI Maine page
facts.fact: The Maine Electricians' Examining Board adopts the NEC statewide by rule (Chapter 120). Under that rule, electrical installations begun on or after July 1, 2024 must follow the 2023 NEC with Maine amendments, such as changes to GFCI rules in 210.8 and to NM cable use in 334.10.
facts.note: Rule text read is current only through June 2025. Mike Holt's list shows Maine on the 2026 NEC effective 7/1/2026, which no official page read confirms. Check the board for the edition in force.

facts.source: 02-395 CMR ch. 4, sec. 1 (Plumbers' Examining Board, Installation Standards) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/maine/02/395/chapter-4/section-395-4-1/
facts.fact: Maine's plumbing installation standard is the 2021 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC), adopted by the Plumbers' Examining Board with exclusions. The board does not adopt the UPC appendices, Chapter 12 (Fuel Gas Piping) or Chapter 13 (Health Care Facilities and Medical Gas), and adopts only listed parts of Chapter 5 (Water Heaters); fuel gas work falls under the Maine Fuel Board.
facts.note: Rule text current through June 2025.

facts.source: IAEI Maryland page - https://www.iaei.org/page/maryland-electrical-ceus; Mike Holt NEC Adoption List
facts.fact: Maryland's statewide NEC edition could not be confirmed from an official state page. IAEI lists the 2023 NEC effective March 1, 2025, while Mike Holt lists the 2020 NEC effective May 29, 2023; many Maryland counties also adopt and enforce the NEC locally.
facts.note: The two trade references disagree, and the State Fire Prevention Code (COMAR 29.06.01.06) incorporates only NFPA 1 and NFPA 101, not NFPA 70. Ask the local jurisdiction which edition it enforces.

facts.source: COMAR 09.20.01.01 (State Board of Plumbing, State Plumbing Code - Incorporation by Reference) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/maryland/title-09/subtitle-20/chapter-09-20-01/section-09-20-01-01/
facts.fact: The Maryland State Plumbing Code (COMAR 09.20.01) incorporates the 2018 International Plumbing Code, the plumbing and fuel gas chapters of the 2018 International Residential Code, the 2018 International Fuel Gas Code and the 2017 edition of NFPA 58, each with Maryland modifications.
facts.note: Rule text current through June 13, 2025; check for a newer adoption.

facts.source: Maryland State Board of HVACR Contractors, Licensing Requirements - https://dllr.state.md.us/license/hvacr/hvacrlicreq.shtml
facts.fact: Maryland's HVACR Limited license requires a journeyman license plus at least 2 years working under a licensed HVACR master, with 1,000 hours in the year before applying, and a 70% score on the limited contractor exam. Master and master restricted licenses instead need 3 years as a journeyman under a master and 1,875 hours in the prior year.

facts.source: IAEI Massachusetts page - https://www.iaei.org/page/massachusetts-electrical-ceus; Mike Holt NEC Adoption List
facts.fact: Massachusetts adopts the NEC statewide as the Massachusetts Electrical Code (527 CMR 12.00), issued by the Board of Fire Prevention Regulations with state amendments. The 2023 NEC took effect February 17, 2023, and a trade reference reports the 2026 NEC took effect April 24, 2026.
facts.note: Mass.gov pages could not be loaded to confirm the edition in force; IAEI shows the 2023 date and Mike Holt shows the 2026 date.

facts.source: 248 CMR chapter list - https://regulations.justia.com/states/massachusetts/248-cmr/; M.G.L. c. 142, sec. 13 - https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleXX/Chapter142/Section13
facts.fact: Massachusetts uses its own state-written Uniform State Plumbing Code (248 CMR 10.00), not the IPC or UPC. The Board of State Examiners of Plumbers and Gas Fitters writes the rules, which apply in all cities and towns; a town's board of health can petition to vary how a rule applies locally. Licensing education and experience standards are in 248 CMR 11.00.

facts.source: 248 CMR chapter list - https://regulations.justia.com/states/massachusetts/248-cmr/
facts.fact: Massachusetts gas fitting follows the Massachusetts Fuel Gas Code in 248 CMR 4.00, with state amendments to NFPA 54 (National Fuel Gas Code) in 248 CMR 5.00 and amendments to NFPA 58 (LP-Gas) in 248 CMR 8.00, all issued by the plumbers and gas fitters board.
facts.note: Chapter titles read; NFPA edition years not confirmed.

facts.source: Mich. Admin. Code R 408.30801 (Part 8 Electrical Code) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/bureau-of-construction-codes/construction-code-commission-general-rules/construction-code/part-8/section-r-408-30801/; IAEI Michigan page
facts.fact: Michigan's Part 8 Electrical Code (R 408.30801) adopts the 2023 NEC (second printing, with TIAs) with some sections excluded. It took effect March 12, 2024 for buildings other than one- and two-family dwellings, which are covered by the Michigan Residential Code.
facts.note: Rule text current through June 2025; effective date from IAEI and Mike Holt, which also say the residential code moved to the 2023 NEC on Aug. 29, 2025.

facts.source: Mich. Admin. Code R 408.30701 (Part 7 Plumbing Code, Applicable code) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/bureau-of-construction-codes/construction-code-commission-general-rules/construction-code/part-7/amendments-and-additions-to-basic-plumbing-code/section-r-408-30701/
facts.fact: Michigan's statewide plumbing code (Part 7, R 408.30701) adopts the 2021 International Plumbing Code (second printing) with Michigan exceptions and amendments, including appendices B, C, D and E.
facts.note: Rule text current through June 2025.

facts.source: Mich. Admin. Code R 408.30901a (Part 9A Mechanical Code) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/bureau-of-construction-codes/construction-code-commission-general-rules/construction-code/part-9a/amendments-and-additions-to-basic-mechanical-code/section-r-408-30901a/
facts.fact: Michigan's statewide mechanical code (Part 9A, R 408.30901a) adopts the 2021 International Mechanical Code by reference, with listed exceptions and Michigan amendments.
facts.note: Rule text current through June 2025.

facts.source: Minnesota DLI, Electrical codes and standards - https://www.dli.mn.gov/business/electrical-contractors/electrical-codes-and-standards
facts.fact: Minnesota's Board of Electricity adopted the 2026 NEC. Electrical permits filed on or after August 17, 2026 must comply with the 2026 NEC, and permits filed before that date follow the 2023 NEC. State electrical licensing exams moved to the 2026 NEC beginning September 8, 2026.

facts.source: Minn. R. 4714.0050 (Minnesota Plumbing Code) - https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/4714.0050/
facts.fact: The Minnesota Plumbing Code (Minn. R. chapter 4714) is based on the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC), adopting chapters 2 to 11, 16 and 17 and appendices A, B and I with Minnesota amendments.
facts.note: Rule as published by the Revisor (2021); check DLI for a newer UPC adoption.

facts.source: Minn. R. 1346.0050 (Minnesota Mechanical Code) - https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/1346.0050/
facts.fact: The Minnesota Mechanical Code (Minn. R. chapter 1346) adopts chapters 2 to 15 of the 2018 International Mechanical Code, subject to Minnesota Rules chapter 1300 and state amendments.
facts.note: Rule as published by the Revisor (April 2020); check DLI for a newer edition.

facts.source: IAEI Mississippi page - https://www.iaei.org/page/mississippi-electrical-ceus; Mike Holt NEC Adoption List
facts.fact: Mississippi has no statewide NEC adoption; electrical codes are adopted locally, so the edition depends on the city or county (for example, Biloxi adopted a 2026 code effective June 1, 2026).
facts.note: IAEI and Mike Holt agree: local adoption only.

facts.source: Miss. Code 31-3-1 - https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-31/chapter-3/section-31-3-1/; Mississippi State Board of Contractors - https://www.msboc.us/
facts.fact: Mississippi does not license journeyman or master electricians, plumbers or HVAC technicians statewide. The Mississippi State Board of Contractors licenses commercial and residential contractors, and its commercial licensing law generally does not apply to contracts under $50,000. Individual trade licenses, where required, come from cities and counties.
facts.note: The $50,000 threshold and board scope were read on official pages; the no-statewide-trade-license point and any separate dollar threshold for electrical, plumbing or mechanical subcontractors were not confirmed.

facts.source: Mike Holt NEC Adoption List - https://www.mikeholt.com/necadoptionlist.php; IAEI Code Adoption by State - https://www.iaei.org/page/nec-code-adoption
facts.fact: Missouri has no statewide NEC adoption; cities and counties adopt and enforce their own electrical code editions. The optional statewide electrical contractor license does not change which code edition applies locally.
facts.note: Mike Holt and IAEI agree: local adoption only.

facts.source: Montana DLI Building and Commercial Measurements Bureau, Current Codes - https://bsd.dli.mt.gov/building-codes-permits/current-codes
facts.fact: Montana's state building codes, adopted in ARM Title 24, Chapter 301, include the 2023 NEC, effective September 26, 2026 (replacing the 2020 NEC, which had been in effect since June 10, 2022).
facts.note: Current-codes page read October 2026; the earlier 2020 date is from IAEI and Mike Holt.

facts.source: Montana DLI Building and Commercial Measurements Bureau, Current Codes - https://bsd.dli.mt.gov/building-codes-permits/current-codes
facts.fact: Montana's state plumbing code is the 2024 Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC), adopted with amendments in ARM Title 24, Chapter 301 and effective September 26, 2026.

facts.source: Montana DLI Building and Commercial Measurements Bureau, Current Codes - https://bsd.dli.mt.gov/building-codes-permits/current-codes
facts.fact: Montana's state mechanical and fuel gas codes are the 2024 International Mechanical Code and 2024 International Fuel Gas Code, effective September 26, 2026, along with the 2024 IBC and IRC.

facts.source: Ala. Admin. Code r. 720-X-4-.01(2) (amended eff. Oct. 13, 2025, operative Jan. 1, 2026) - https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/720-X-4; r. 720-X-5-.01
facts.fact: In Alabama, a journeyman plumber or journeyman gas fitter needs 2 years of current work experience as an apprentice (or completion of a board-approved apprentice program), and a master plumber or master gas fitter needs 1 year of current experience as a journeyman, with verifiable proof. A journeyman plumber works under the general supervision of a certified master plumber.

facts.source: Ala. Admin. Code r. 303-X-4-.02 and -.08 (eff. Feb. 14, 2026) - https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/303-X-4
facts.fact: Alabama certified electrical contractors must earn 14 hours of continuing education in each two-year cycle. Hours are credited in 2-hour blocks (one hour = at least 50 minutes), up to 7 hours can roll over, and a contractor is exempt from the 14 hours for the first renewal after initial licensing.
facts.note: The rule also refers to completing requirements 'annually' in one paragraph; check the board's CE calendar (existing KB fact STAT-011 notes 2027 is a CE year).

facts.source: Ala. Admin. Code r. 303-X-1-.01 (eff. Feb. 14, 2026) - https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/303-X-1
facts.fact: Alabama Electrical Contractors Board rules treat the term 'electrical contractor' as interchangeable with 'master electrician.' A journeyman electrician must work under a master or state-certified electrical contractor, and an inactive contractor or journeyman cannot buy local licenses or pull permits.

facts.source: Alabama HACR Board rule 440-X-3-.04 - https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/chapter/440-X-3
facts.fact: Alabama HVACR certification can be earned by exam or by reciprocity (for licensees from reciprocal states with no past or pending discipline). An applicant who fails the exam the first time may retake it, or request a practical exam, within six months of the failed attempt.

facts.source: Georgia SOS, Division of Master and Journeyman Plumbers FAQ - https://sos.ga.gov/page/division-master-and-journeyman-plumbers-faq
facts.fact: Georgia plumbing license exams are given by PSI on a continuous basis at various locations. A candidate who fails twice must submit a certificate of completion from a board-approved review course before testing again.

facts.source: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 121-3-.01 - https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/georgia/Ga-Comp-R-Regs-R-121-3-.01
facts.fact: Georgia electrical contractor applicants must submit three references, at least one from a licensed electrical contractor. Instead of documenting primary experience, an applicant with 6 years of electrical contracting experience may qualify with a reference from a licensed architect, professional engineer or electrical engineer; up to 1 year of secondary experience counts at 50%.

facts.source: 02-658 CMR ch. 6, sec. 1 (Maine Fuel Board, Adopted Standards) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/maine/02/658/chapter-6/section-658-6-1/
facts.fact: The Maine Fuel Board adopts NFPA standards for fuel-burning equipment, including NFPA 31 (oil-burning equipment, 2020 edition), NFPA 54 National Fuel Gas Code (2021), NFPA 58 LP-Gas Code (2020), NFPA 211 chimneys and vents (2019) and NFPA 90B warm-air heating and AC systems (2021), each with Maine exclusions and amendments where listed.
facts.note: Rule text current through June 2025.

facts.source: Minn. R. 1346.5050 (Minnesota Fuel Gas Code) - https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/1346.5050/
facts.fact: The Minnesota Fuel Gas Code incorporates Chapters 2 to 8 of the 2018 International Fuel Gas Code by reference, as part of the Minnesota Mechanical and Fuel Gas Code (Minn. R. chapter 1346).
facts.note: Rule as published by the Revisor (April 2020).

facts.source: Idaho H0478 (2024), Session Law Chapter 54, signed March 18, 2024 - https://legiscan.com/ID/bill/H0478/2024; Idaho Code 54-2601
facts.fact: A 2024 Idaho law (H0478, signed March 18, 2024) amended state law to provide for local enforcement of the Idaho electrical code and the Idaho plumbing code, so a city or county can run its own electrical and plumbing permits and inspections instead of the state DOPL.
facts.note: Based on the bill summary and status as recorded on LegiScan; full bill text not read.

facts.source: Montana DLI Building Codes Program - https://bsd.dli.mt.gov/building-codes-permits/
facts.fact: In Montana, cities, counties and towns may choose to enforce building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical codes, but their programs must be certified by the state Building Codes Program. Areas that do not enforce codes fall under state jurisdiction, and state agencies' projects are always permitted through the state.

facts.source: 17 CAR 261-103(e) and 261-104(b)(1) - https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/17CARpt.261-Clean.pdf
facts.fact: Arkansas offers a Class L lifetime HVACR license for service and maintenance only, on air conditioning of 15 tons or less per unit and refrigeration of 15 hp or less per unit. To get it, a licensee must be at least 65 and have held a board license for 10 consecutive years.
facts.note: Read in the DOLL-posted 17 CAR Part 261 rule text (clean copy).

facts.source: Mich. Admin. Code R 408.30536 (Part 5 Residential Code, electrical) - https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/bureau-of-construction-codes/construction-code-commission-general-rules/construction-code/part-5/section-r-408-30536/
facts.fact: For one- and two-family dwellings, the Michigan Residential Code uses the IRC electrical chapters (34 to 43) with Michigan amendments, and any electrical item not covered there must comply with the Michigan Electrical Code (R 408.30801 to R 408.30880). Solar PV systems must follow NFPA 70.
facts.note: Rule text current through June 2025.

questions.q: Under Alabama Electrical Contractors Board rules effective in 2026, how many hours of electrical experience must a journeyman electrician applicant document?
questions.why: Alabama requires a minimum of 8,000 hours for journeyman (and contractor) applicants; up to 2,000 hours can come from apprenticeship or education.

questions.q: Which NEC edition does 8 AAC 70.025 adopt as Alaska's statewide minimum electrical code?
questions.why: Alaska's regulation adopts the 2020 edition of NFPA 70 as the minimum electrical code for the state.

questions.q: How many years of experience does the Arizona Registrar of Contractors require of the qualifying party for a C-37 plumbing license?
questions.why: The ROC classification table lists 4 years of hands-on and/or managerial experience for C-37 (and for R-37 and CR-37).

questions.q: The 2025 California Electrical Code, effective January 1, 2026, is based on which NEC edition?
questions.why: The state's rulemaking says the 2025 CEC is based on the 2023 NEC, effective January 1, 2026.

questions.q: Which model code is the 2025 California Plumbing Code based on?
questions.why: California bases its plumbing code on IAPMO's Uniform Plumbing Code; the 2025 CPC adopts the 2024 UPC.

questions.q: How many hours of experience does California's DIR require for General Electrician certification?
questions.why: General Electrician needs 8,000 hours; Residential Electrician needs 4,800.

questions.q: An Arkansas Class B HVACR license is limited to air conditioning systems of no more than how much cooling capacity per unit?
questions.why: Class B covers AC systems of 25 tons or less per unit (and heating up to 1,000,000 BTUH input); Class A has no limit.

questions.q: Which plumbing code has the Colorado State Plumbing Board adopted as the statewide plumbing code?
questions.why: Colorado's plumbing board incorporates the 2021 IPC (with the 2021 IFGC) by reference, with Colorado amendments.

questions.q: In Connecticut, how much experience as a licensed unlimited journeyperson does an E-1 Unlimited Electrical Contractor applicant need?
questions.why: E-1 requires 2 years as an unlimited licensed journeyperson, or 6 years of equivalent experience and training.

questions.q: Which edition of the International Plumbing Code does the State of Delaware Plumbing Code (16 Del. Admin. Code 4455) adopt?
questions.why: Delaware's Division of Public Health adopted the 2021 IPC with amendments, effective August 11, 2022.

questions.q: The DC Electrical Code in the 2017 DC Construction Codes (effective May 29, 2020) is based on which NEC edition?
questions.why: DOB lists the 2014 NEC as the model code for 12C DCMR, even though the package is called the 2017 codes.

questions.q: A Florida Class B air-conditioning contractor is limited to which system size?
c: 25 tons of cooling and 500,000 Btu of heating in any one system
15 tons of cooling and 250,000 Btu of heating in any one system
50 tons of cooling and 1,000,000 Btu of heating in any one system
10 tons of cooling and 100,000 Btu of heating in any one system
questions.why: Class B is limited to 25 tons of cooling and 500,000 Btu of heating per system; Class A is unlimited.

questions.q: When does the 9th Edition (2026) Florida Building Code, which moves Florida to the 2023 NEC, take effect?
questions.why: The Commission's schedule sets the 9th Edition effective date at December 31, 2026, six months after publication.

questions.q: A Georgia Class I (restricted) electrical contractor is limited to single-phase installations that do not exceed how many amperes at the service drop or lateral?
questions.why: Class I covers single-phase work not over 200 amps; Class II is unrestricted.

questions.q: A Georgia Conditioned Air Contractor Class I license covers systems up to 175,000 BTU of heating and how much cooling?
questions.why: The restricted Class I limit is 175,000 BTU heating and 60,000 BTU (5 tons) cooling.

questions.q: Under HRS 448E-5, how many hours of experience does a Hawaii journey worker electrician applicant need?
questions.why: Hawaii requires 5 years and at least 10,000 hours of supervised wiring experience, plus 240 hours of coursework.

questions.q: Idaho's DOPL moved to which NEC edition effective April 19, 2024?
questions.why: DOPL transitioned to the 2023 NEC on April 19, 2024; permits issued earlier are inspected under the 2017 NEC.

questions.q: Who has the power to set Illinois's minimum statewide plumbing code?
c: The Illinois Department of Public Health
The International Association of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials
questions.ref: 77 Ill. Adm. Code 890; Plumbing License Law Sec. 42
questions.why: IDPH writes the Illinois Plumbing Code, and that power cannot be taken over by local governments, even home-rule units.

questions.q: How are electricians licensed in Indiana?
c: By a state electrical licensing board
Only by cities and counties; there is no statewide electrician license
By the Indiana Department of Health
questions.why: Indiana has no statewide electrician license; local jurisdictions such as Indianapolis handle licensing.

questions.q: Which plumbing code became Iowa's state plumbing code on March 26, 2025?
questions.why: Iowa's board adopted the 2024 UPC with amendments, effective March 26, 2025, replacing the 2021 UPC.

questions.q: Under K.S.A. 12-1526, what minimum score is needed to pass a Kansas local electrician licensing exam?
questions.why: Kansas sets a 75% minimum passing score for the designated standard electrician exams.

questions.q: When did Kentucky begin mandatory enforcement of the 2023 NEC?
questions.why: Enforcement began January 1, 2025; a few dwelling rules (like 230.67) were delayed to July 15, 2026.

questions.q: In 2016, what replaced the Louisiana State Plumbing Code as Louisiana's plumbing code?
questions.why: The LUCCC states that on January 1, 2016 the ICC's IPC replaced the Louisiana State Plumbing Code.

questions.q: Which chapter of the 2021 UPC does Maine's Plumbers' Examining Board NOT adopt?
questions.why: Maine adopts the 2021 UPC but excludes Chapter 12 (Fuel Gas Piping), Chapter 13 and the appendices.

questions.q: Which model plumbing code does the Maryland State Plumbing Code (COMAR 09.20.01) incorporate?
questions.why: Maryland incorporates the 2018 IPC (plus parts of the 2018 IRC, the 2018 IFGC and NFPA 58) with state modifications.

questions.q: What is Massachusetts's plumbing code based on?
c: Its own state-written Uniform State Plumbing Code (248 CMR 10.00)
questions.why: Massachusetts writes its own Uniform State Plumbing Code through the Board of State Examiners of Plumbers and Gas Fitters.

questions.q: Michigan's Part 7 Plumbing Code (R 408.30701) adopts which model code?
questions.why: Michigan adopts the 2021 IPC (second printing) with state exceptions and amendments.

questions.q: In Minnesota, electrical permits filed on or after August 17, 2026 must comply with which NEC edition?
questions.ref: MN DLI Electrical codes and standards
questions.why: Minnesota's Board of Electricity adopted the 2026 NEC for permits filed on or after August 17, 2026; earlier permits follow the 2023 NEC.

questions.q: How is the NEC adopted in Mississippi?
c: Statewide by the State Fire Marshal
Statewide by the State Board of Contractors
Locally, by each city or county
Statewide by the Department of Health
questions.ref: IAEI Mississippi; Mike Holt NEC list
questions.why: Mississippi has no statewide NEC adoption; cities and counties adopt their own editions.

questions.q: Which plumbing code took effect statewide in Montana on September 26, 2026?
questions.why: Montana adopted the 2024 UPC (with the 2023 NEC and 2024 IMC/IFGC), effective September 26, 2026.

questions.q: Which mechanical code did Iowa adopt as its state mechanical code effective March 26, 2025?
questions.why: Iowa adopted Sections 101-102 and Chapters 2-15 of the 2024 IMC, effective March 26, 2025.

questions.q: In Alabama, how much current experience as a journeyman plumber does a master plumber applicant need?
questions.why: Alabama requires 1 year of current work experience as a journeyman plumber; journeyman applicants need 2 years as an apprentice.

questions.q: Which edition of NFPA 54, the National Fuel Gas Code, has the Maine Fuel Board adopted?
questions.why: The Maine Fuel Board's adopted standards list NFPA 54 (2021 edition), with Maine exclusions and amendments.
